claim: Plasmodium falciparum causes placental malaria, which results in adverse outcomes for mother and child.
source: Plasmodium falciparum causes placental malaria, which results in adverse outcomes for mother and child.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as background information and is supported by established scientific knowledge about malaria in pregnancy.

claim: P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes that express the parasite protein VAR2CSA on their surface can bind to placental chondroitin sulfate A.
source: P. falciparum-infected erythrocytes that express the parasite protein VAR2CSA on their surface can bind to placental chondroitin sulfate A.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction.

claim: It has been hypothesized that naturally acquired antibodies towards VAR2CSA protect against placental infection.
source: It has been hypothesized that naturally acquired antibodies towards VAR2CSA protect against placental infection, but it has proven difficult to identify robust antibody correlates of protection from disease.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis in the abstract and is supported by literature references.

claim: Machine learning techniques selected 6 out of 169 measured antibody features towards VAR2CSA that could predict whether a woman would subsequently have active placental malaria infection at delivery with 86% accuracy.
source: The machine learning techniques selected 6 out of 169 measured antibody features towards VAR2CSA that could predict (with 86% accuracy) whether a woman would subsequently have active placental malaria infection at delivery.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Five of the six leading antibody features identified were related to inhibition of placental binding and/or opsonic phagocytosis of infected erythrocytes.
source: Five of the six leading antibody features we found were related to inhibition of placental sequestration and/or opsonization for phagocytic clearance.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a result and is supported by the analysis presented in the results section.

claim: There are multiple pathways to protection against placental malaria.
source: It is likely that there are multiple pathways to protection against placental malaria.
evidence: This conclusion is stated in the abstract and supported by network analysis and heat map data showing varied antibody profiles in protected women.

claim: The burden of Plasmodium falciparum malaria is greatest in young children and pregnant women.
source: The burden of Plasmodium falciparum malaria is greatest in young children and pregnant women (World Health Organisation, 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to WHO 2019.

claim: Pregnant women have increased susceptibility to malaria, and complications include maternal mortality, severe maternal anemia, miscarriage and stillbirth, and impaired fetal growth or prematurity leading to low birth weight delivery.
source: Among women with lifelong malaria exposure, pregnant women have increased susceptibility to malaria, and complications include maternal mortality, severe maternal anemia, miscarriage and stillbirth, and impaired fetal growth or prematurity leading to low birth weight delivery (Steketee et al., 2001; Guyatt and Snow, 2001; Desai et al., 2007; Moore et al., 2017a; Moore et al., 2017b).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with multiple supporting citations.

claim: The prevalence, intensity, and consequences of infection decline with increasing gravidity.
source: The prevalence, intensity, and consequences of infection decline with increasing gravidity (Guyatt and Snow, 2001).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The susceptibility of pregnant women to P. falciparum malaria is in part due to the ability of infected erythrocytes to sequester in the maternal blood spaces of the placenta.
source: The susceptibility of pregnant women to P. falciparum malaria is in part due to the ability of infected erythrocytes (IEs) to sequester in the maternal blood spaces of the placenta (Rogerson et al., 2007), where IEs that express VAR2CSA adhere to chondroitin sulfate A (CSA), a glycosaminoglycan chain on syndecan-1 expressed by the placental syncytiotrophoblast (Salanti et al., 2004; Ayres Pereira et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: VAR2CSA is a unique 350 kDa protein that is a member of the P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1) family of variant surface antigens.
source: VAR2CSA is a unique 350 kDa protein that is a member of the P. falciparum erythrocyte membrane protein 1 (PfEMP1) family of variant surface antigens (VSA).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as established knowledge about VAR2CSA structure.

claim: VAR2CSA has six DBL domains, with CSA adhesion being strongly associated with the DBL2 domain.
source: VAR2CSA has six DBL domains, with CSA adhesion being strongly associated with the DBL2 domain, which is present in the N-terminal region of the protein (Doritchamou et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Two constructs based on the N-terminal region of VAR2CSA have entered clinical trials as vaccine candidates to prevent placental malaria.
source: Two constructs based on this region have entered clinical trials as vaccine candidates to prevent placental malaria (Mordmüller et al., 2019; Sirima et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations to clinical trial publications.

claim: Antibodies to VAR2CSA develop in a parity-dependent manner.
source: Antibodies to VAR2CSA, in its native form on IE or expressed as recombinant protein, develop in a parity-dependent manner, block adhesion to CSA, and opsonize IE for phagocytosis by monocytic cells (Fried et al., 1998; Ricke et al., 2000; Salanti et al., 2004; Keen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Antibodies to VAR2CSA block adhesion to CSA and opsonize IE for phagocytosis by monocytic cells.
source: Antibodies to VAR2CSA, in its native form on IE or expressed as recombinant protein, develop in a parity-dependent manner, block adhesion to CSA, and opsonize IE for phagocytosis by monocytic cells (Fried et al., 1998; Ricke et al., 2000; Salanti et al., 2004; Keen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Some studies report associations between measures of single antibody features and protection from malaria complications such as placental infection, impaired fetal growth, prematurity, or anemia.
source: Some studies report associations between measures of single antibody features and protection from malaria complications such as placental infection, impaired fetal growth, prematurity, or anemia (Duffy and Fried, 2003; Staalsoe et al., 2004; Feng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Identifying targets and features of protective antibody responses to malaria is challenging because exposure to infection is accompanied by the production of antibody to many parasite antigens, only a fraction of which contributes to protective immunity.
source: However, identifying targets and features of protective antibody responses to malaria is challenging because exposure to infection is accompanied by the production of antibody to many parasite antigens, only a fraction of which contributes to protective immunity (Crompton et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Antibody responses to VAR2CSA were often correlated with exposure to placental malaria, rather than protection from infection.
source: In a recent systematic review, antibody responses to VAR2CSA were often correlated with exposure to placental malaria, rather than protection from infection (Cutts et al., 2020), although some studies indicate an association between antibody to IE and protection from low birth weight in subsets of pregnant women (Duffy and Fried, 2003; Staalsoe et al., 2004; Feng et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation to a systematic review.

claim: Study participants were recruited between November 2009 and August 2012 as part of a randomized controlled trial of Intermittent Preventive Treatment in Pregnancy.
source: Study participants were recruited between November 2009 and August 2012 as part of a randomized controlled trial of Intermittent Preventive Treatment in Pregnancy (IPTp) (Unger et al., 2015) (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01136850), in which pregnant women received either three courses of sulfadoxine pyrimethamine (SP) and azithromycin or one course of SP and chloroquine.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the study cohort.

claim: Women were recruited at 14–26 gestation weeks and followed up until delivery.
source: Women were recruited at 14–26 gestation weeks and followed up until delivery.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the study design.

claim: The cohort comprised 50 women who subsequently had no P. falciparum parasites detected on placental histology and were PCR negative for peripheral parasitemia at delivery (non-infected), 50 women who had P. falciparum parasites in the placenta by histology (placental malaria), and 27 women who had no P. falciparum parasites in the placenta by histology but who had peripheral blood parasitemia by PCR and/or light microscopy (non-placental infection) at delivery.
source: The cohort comprised 50 women who subsequently had no P. falciparum parasites detected on placental histology and were PCR negative for peripheral parasitemia at delivery (non-infected), 50 women who had P. falciparum parasites in the placenta by histology (placental malaria), and 27 women who had no P. falciparum parasites in the placenta by histology but who had peripheral blood parasitemia by PCR and/or light microscopy (non-placental infection) at delivery.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the cohort composition.

claim: The three groups were frequency matched for primigravidity, IPTp regime receipt, bed net use, rural residency, and age.
source: The three groups were frequency matched for primigravidity, IPTp regime receipt, bed net use, rural residency, and age, and all three groups had similar clinical characteristics at enrollment (Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the study design.

claim: Thirteen features of antibody towards recombinant forms of each of the six DBL domains were measured by multiplex in the 127 women.
source: Thirteen features of antibody towards recombinant forms of each of the six DBL domains were measured by multiplex in the 127 women.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the antibody measurements.

claim: Antibody features measured by multiplex included antibody isotypes (IgG, IgA, IgM) and subclasses (IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, IgG4, IgA1, IgA2), and the ability of antigen-specific antibody to bind Fcy receptors (FcyR) and complement protein C1q.
source: Antibody features measured by multiplex included antibody isotypes (IgG, IgA, IgM) and subclasses (IgG1, IgG2, IgG3, IgG4, IgA1, IgA2), and the ability of antigen-specific antibody to bind Fcy receptors (FcyR) and complement protein C1q (which assesses the ability of antibodies to activate the classical complement cascade).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the antibody measurements.

claim: Levels of antibody features measured by multiplex were similar between non-infected women at delivery and those with placental malaria.
source: Notably, levels of antibody to DBL domains at enrollment were similar between non-infected women at delivery and those with placental malaria (Figure 1A)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1A showing volcano plot comparisons.

claim: Multiple antibody features were higher in women with non-placental infection than in placental malaria, indicating potential roles in protection.
source: whereas multiple antibody features were higher in women with non-placental infection than in placental malaria, indicating potential roles in protection (Figure 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1B showing volcano plot comparisons.

claim: IgG levels to neither MSP-1 nor schizont extract were higher in women without placental malaria.
source: IgG levels to neither MSP-1 nor schizont extract were higher in women without placental malaria (Supplementary file 2), suggesting that differences in antibody to pregnancy specific antigens were not simply due to exposure.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to supplementary data.

claim: The ENLR model was repeatedly fitted to randomly resampled subsets of the data and the selection frequency and the effect size (odds ratio) of the antibody features were calculated.
source: Initially, the ENLR model was repeatedly fitted to randomly resampled subsets of the data and the selection frequency and the effect size (odds ratio) of the antibody features were calculated (Figure 2)
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the statistical analysis approach.

claim: The mean AUROC and accuracy of classifying women with non-placental infection do not increase significantly after the inclusion of the six top features.
source: The mean AUROC and accuracy of classifying women with non-placental infection do not increase significantly after the inclusion of the six top features (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3A.

claim: The model with the six selected features performed significantly better than the PLSDA models with randomly selected features.
source: The results show that the model with the six selected features performed significantly better than the PLSDA models with randomly selected features.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the validation of the model.

claim: The AUROC for the six features corresponds to a median accuracy of 0.86.
source: The AUROC for the six features corresponds to a median accuracy of 0.86 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) and means that the model with these six antibody features can accurately classify, on average, 86% of the women.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with reference to a supplementary figure.

claim: The six selected features included IgG3 to DBL2, ADCP and ADNP of CSA-binding IE, binding inhibition of IE to CSA, IgA2 to DBL2, and IgG3 to CSA binding IE.
source: The six selected features included IgG3 to DBL2 (IgG3.DBL2(ID1-ID2a).FCR3), ADCP, and ADNP of CSA-binding IE (THP1.Phago.CS2 and Neutrophil.Phago.CS2, respectively), binding inhibition of IE to CSA (CSA.Binding.Inhibition.FCR3), IgA2 to DBL2 (IgA2.DBL2.1010), and IgG3 to CSA binding IE (IgG3.3D7).
evidence: This is stated in the results section listing the identified features.

claim: For all six features, antibody levels were significantly higher in the non-placental infection group compared to the placental malaria group.
source: For all six features, antibody levels were significantly higher in the non-placental infection group compared to the placental malaria group (Figure 5A–F)
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5A-F showing individual feature comparisons.

claim: 81% of women with non-placental infection had a Z-score >0 for at least four antibody features compared to 26% of those with placental malaria.
source: Overall, the women with non-placental infection had significantly higher levels of most of the identified antibody features; 81% of women with non-placental infection had a Z-score >0 for at least four antibody features (compared to 26% of those with placental malaria).
evidence: This is stated in the results section analyzing the heat map data.

claim: 52% of women with non-placental infection had elevated antibodies that both promoted IE phagocytosis by THP-1 cells and/or neutrophils and inhibited binding of IE to CSA, compared to 18% of women with placental malaria.
source: Looking at just the three functional measures, 52% of women with non-placental infection had elevated antibodies (a Z-score >0) that both promoted IE phagocytosis by THP-1 cells and/or neutrophils and inhibited binding of IE to CSA, compared to 18% of women with placental malaria (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section analyzing functional antibody features.

claim: The six features identified by ENLR + PLSDA were spread throughout the correlation network and were not well correlated with each other.
source: Importantly, the six features identified by ENLR + PLSDA were spread throughout the correlation network and were not well correlated with each other (Figure 4, Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the correlation network figure.

claim: The ability of antibodies to inhibit binding of IE to CSA was the only antibody feature with evidence of a positive association with gravidity in this cohort.
source: Ability of antibodies to inhibit binding of IE to CSA (CSA.Binding.Inhibition.FCR3) was the only antibody feature with evidence of a positive association with gravidity in this cohort (p=0.046).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing univariate linear regression analysis.

claim: Four of the six antibody features were significantly higher in the non-placental infection cohort when excluding women infected at enrollment.
source: Importantly, four of the six antibody features were significantly higher in the non-placental infection cohort (p≤0.013), and the remaining two features trended to be higher in the non-placental cohort (p≤0.064).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing a subanalysis excluding women with early infections.

claim: The ability to block IE binding to CSA has been associated with protection against placental malaria, maternal anemia, low birth weight, or prematurity in subsets of pregnant women.
source: The ability to block IE binding to CSA has been associated with protection against placental malaria, maternal anemia, low birth weight, or prematurity in subsets of pregnant women (Duffy and Fried, 2003; Ndam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: IgG1 and IgG3 antibody responses to VAR2CSA are dominant and mediate opsonic clearance of IE.
source: IgG1 and IgG3 antibody responses to VAR2CSA are dominant and mediate opsonic clearance of IE (Tebo et al., 2002; Elliott et al., 2005a; Megnekou et al., 2005; Keen et al., 2007; Damelang et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: ADCP using THP-1 cells has been correlated with protection from malaria or its complications in pregnant women and in adults.
source: ADCP using THP-1 cells has been correlated with protection from malaria or its complications in pregnant women and in adults (reviewed in Teo et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to a review.

claim: IgA2 can elicit myeloid cell effector functions, including opsonic phagocytosis mediated by FcαRI.
source: IgA2 can elicit myeloid cell effector functions, including opsonic phagocytosis (mediated by FcαRI) (Breedveld and van Egmond, 2019)
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: A recent study looking for correlates of malaria protection from vaccine-induced immunity also identified IgA2 as a variable that helped predict those protected from P. falciparum infection.
source: Interestingly a recent study looking for correlates of malaria protection from vaccine-induced immunity also identified IgA2 as a variable that helped predict those protected from P. falciparum infection (Suscovich et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Vaccination with VAR2CSA-based vaccines offered limited heterologous protection.
source: Vaccination offered limited heterologous protection (Sirima et al., 2020), and it is unclear whether effective naturally acquired protective immunity needs to target multiple clades or different clades in different regions.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: Antibody to VAR2CSA recombinant proteins, and particularly to specific VAR2CSA peptides, appears to be a good correlate of exposure and transmission intensity.
source: Antibody to VAR2CSA recombinant proteins, and particularly to specific VAR2CSA peptides, appears to be a good correlate of exposure and transmission intensity (Fonseca et al., 2019), but these responses appear to be less useful as correlates of protection.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a supporting citation.

claim: The correlation network showed close correlations between different antibody responses to recombinant DBL domains but the protective antibody features were dispersed.
source: The correlation network showed close correlations between different antibody responses to recombinant DBL domains (which are predominantly located in the central cluster) but the protective antibody features were dispersed, suggesting that distinct pathways contribute to the development of protection against placental malaria.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the correlation network analysis in Figure 4.

claim: Most protected women had significant antibody that promoted both binding inhibition to CSA and phagocytosis, but no consistent pattern of antibody functions in protected women was seen.
source: The analysis of functions identified in the selected features further supports this, with most protected women (and few unprotected women) having significant antibody that promoted both binding inhibition to CSA and phagocytosis; however, no consistent pattern of antibody functions in protected women was seen.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by the heat map analysis in Figure 5G.

claim: Placental malaria was defined by the detection of IE in the placenta by histology because previous studies have shown that these are the infections associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes.
source: We were interested in measuring antibodies to placental binding parasites and defined placental malaria by the detection of IE in the placenta by histology because previous studies have shown that these are the infections associated with adverse pregnancy outcomes (Menendez et al., 2000; Rogerson et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Study strengths include the application of 169 novel and established assays, minimal missing predictor and no missing outcome data, the ability to control for exposure with the identification of pregnant women with P. falciparum infection with and without placental malaria, the prospective study design, and the use of native antigens on IEs to complement the data acquired using recombinant protein.
source: Study strengths include the application of 169 novel and established assays; minimal missing predictor and no missing outcome data, the ability to control for exposure with the identification of pregnant women with P. falciparum infection with, and without, placental malaria; the prospective study design; and the use of native antigens on IEs to complement the data we acquired using recombinant protein.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion describing study strengths.

claim: Weaknesses include the lack of inclusion of full-length VAR2CSA in Luminex and bead-based assays, and an imbalance in numbers between women with parasitemia but no placental infection relative to the other groups.
source: Weaknesses include the lack of inclusion of full-length VAR2CSA in our Luminex and bead-based assays, and an imbalance in numbers between women with parasitemia but no placental infection relative to the other groups.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion describing study limitations.

claim: The present study identified leading candidate antibody features that mediate naturally acquired protection from placental malaria and demonstrated these features could identify women in this cohort protected from placental malaria with high accuracy.
source: The present study identified leading candidate antibody features that mediate naturally acquired protection from placental malaria and demonstrated we could use these features to identify women in this cohort protected from placental malaria with high accuracy (though this should be validated in a second cohort).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of findings.

claim: The results suggest that multiple pathways exist that lead to the development of protective immunity against placental malaria.
source: Our results suggest that multiple pathways exist that lead to the development of protective immunity against placental malaria.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the data.

claim: The immune responses identified are relevant to further development of pregnancy malaria-specific therapies such as vaccines or monoclonal antibodies.
source: The immune responses identified are relevant to further development of pregnancy malaria-specific therapies such as vaccines or monoclonal antibodies and possibly to the identification of protective antibody against malaria in non-pregnant populations.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an implication of the findings.

claim: Multiple antibody functions and characteristics may be required to develop robust protective immunity to placental malaria.
source: Multiple antibody functions and characteristics may be required to develop robust protective immunity to placental malaria.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the findings.

claim: The segregation of the observations by the PLSDA was largely driven by the top two variables identified by ENLR: DBL2-specific IgG3 and ADCP of the CSA-binding IE CS2 by THP1.
source: The loading components illustrate that the segregation of the observations by the PLSDA was largely driven by the top two variables identified by ENLR, DBL2-specific IgG3 (IgG3.DBL2(ID1-ID2a).FCR3), and ADCP of the CSA-binding IE CS2 by THP1 (THP1.Phago.CS2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the PLSDA analysis and is supported by Figure 3D.

claim: Using samples from the 127 women and measuring 13 antibody features directed at 10 DBL domains, 15,340 out of 16,510 possible data points were acquired.
source: Thus, using samples from the 127 women and measuring 13 antibody features directed at 10 DBL domains, 15,340 out of 16,510 possible data points were acquired (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2 for a flow chart of data acquisition).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the data acquisition.

claim: With 39 variables for 77 women, 2997 measurements (99.8% of possible 3003) were acquired for IE and leukocyte antibody features.
source: With 39 variables for 77 women, 2997 measurements (99.8% of possible 3003) were acquired.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the data acquisition for cellular assays.

claim: When multiplex and cellular assay data were combined, 169 variables with a total of 12,906 measurements (99.2% of 13,013) were used in subsequent analyses.
source: When added to the multiplex data, 169 variables with a total of 12,906 measurements (99.2% of 13,013) were used in subsequent analyses (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1 for the flow chart).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the complete dataset.

claim: None of the women had any data missing for the outcome variable, and 11 out of 77 women had data missing for one or more of the 169 predictor variables.
source: None of the women had any data missing for the outcome variable, and 11 out of 77 women had data missing for one or more of the 169 predictor variables.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing missing data.

claim: All clinical data were collected, and grouping of women by outcome was completed prior to measurements of antibody features included in the model.
source: All clinical data were collected, and grouping of women by outcome was completed prior to measurements of antibody features included in the model.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the study design to minimize bias.

claim: Researchers measuring antibody features were blinded to outcome data of individual samples.
source: Researchers measuring antibody features were blinded to outcome data of individual samples; this was done by allocating all samples a number (which was not associated with clinical outcomes and which was different from the original cohort study number), samples were decoded after acquisition of the antibody feature was complete.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing blinding procedures.

claim: The CSA-binding phenotypes of CS2 and 3D7 IEs were monitored by measuring binding of trophozoite stage IEs in static binding assays to recombinant human CD36 and CSA.
source: The CSA-binding phenotypes of CS2 and 3D7 IEs were monitored by measuring binding of trophozoite stage IEs in static binding assays to recombinant human CD36 (R&D systems, Noble Park, Australia) and CSA (Sigma-Aldrich, Macquarie Park, Australia) as previously described (Yosaatmadja et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing parasite characterization.

claim: 3D7 was selected for a CSA-binding phenotype by flow cytometry.
source: 3D7 was selected for a CSA-binding phenotype by flow cytometry.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing parasite selection procedures.

claim: Multivariate imputations by chained equations with predictive mean matching was used to impute any missing values (0.82% of observations).
source: Multivariate imputations by chained equations (Buuren and Groothuis-Oudshoorn, 2011) with predictive mean matching was used to impute any missing values (0.82% of observations).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing data processing.

claim: A resampling approach was used in which the ENLR model was repeatedly fitted to subsets of data, providing a means to take account of the uncertainty in the feature selection.
source: We used a resampling approach in which the ENLR model was repeatedly fitted to subsets of data, as used by Gunn et al., 2018. This provided a means to take account of the uncertainty in the feature selection by ENLR and identify the features that are consistently selected when the model is fitted to different resampled data.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the statistical approach with a citation.

claim: The selection stability of an antibody feature was defined as the proportion of times that it was picked in the selected set of important features by elastic net when the model was repeatedly fitted to 50,000 resampled subsets of data.
source: The selection stability of an antibody feature was defined as the proportion of times that it was picked in the selected set of important features by elastic net when the model was repeatedly fitted to 50,000 resampled subsets of data (5000 repeats of 10-fold cross-validation).
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the feature selection approach.

claim: In each resampling iteration, the majority group (50 women with placental malaria) was downsampled to have an equal number of observations in both groups, thus avoiding overfitting the model to the majority group.
source: In each resampling iteration, the majority group (50 women with placental malaria) was downsampled to have an equal number of observations in both groups, thus avoiding overfitting the model to the majority group.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the resampling procedure.

claim: Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLSDA) was subsequently applied on the results of the ENLR to reassert the set of selected antibody features and find a minimal set of antibody features that accurately classifies the pregnant women.
source: Partial least squares discriminant analysis (PLSDA) (Barker and Rayens, 2003) was subsequently applied on the results of the ENLR to reassert the set of selected antibody features and find a minimal set of antibody features that accurately classifies the pregnant women
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the statistical analysis approach with a citation.

claim: The antibody features were added to the PLSDA model one by one, from the highest to lowest selection frequency as estimated by the ENLR, and the minimal set of features beyond which the accuracy did not improve significantly were selected as the final set of key antibody features.
source: The antibody features were added to the PLSDA model one by one, from the highest to lowest selection frequency as estimated by the ENLR, and the minimal set of features beyond which the accuracy did not improve significantly were selected as the final set of key antibody features (Gunn et al., 2018)
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the feature selection procedure with a citation.

claim: 500 repeats of 10-fold cross-validation were performed to compute the accuracies.
source: 500 repeats of 10-fold cross-validation were performed to compute the accuracies.
evidence: This is stated in the methods section describing the validation procedure.

claim: The frequently selected antibody features were positively associated with non-placental infection.
source: The frequently selected antibody features were positively associated with non-placental infection (Figure 2B), and the effect of the antibody features on the odds of belonging to the non-placental infection group increased as the selection frequency increased.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B showing odds ratios.

claim: The effect of the antibody features on the odds of belonging to the non-placental infection group increased as the selection frequency increased.
source: The frequently selected antibody features were positively associated with non-placental infection (Figure 2B), and the effect of the antibody features on the odds of belonging to the non-placental infection group increased as the selection frequency increased.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B.

claim: The AUROC is significantly higher than that of the permutation test where the group labels were randomly permuted.
source: The AUROC is also significantly higher than that of the permutation test where the group labels were randomly permuted (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3B showing permutation test results.

claim: Within the non-placental infection and placental malaria cohorts, there was significant variation in individual profiles and no evidence for a unique and consistent profile of antibody functions in all individuals with non-placental infection.
source: Within these two cohorts, there was significant variation in individual profiles and no evidence for a unique and consistent profile of antibody functions in all individuals with non-placental infection.
evidence: This is stated in the results section analyzing the heat map data in Figure 5G.

claim: Some women in the non-placental infection group had no measurable levels of THP1.phago.CS2, IgG3.3D7 or IgG2.DBL5.0466 antibody, indicating that there are multiple mechanisms for antibodies to confer protection.
source: For example, some women in the non-placental infection group had no measurable levels of THP1.phago.CS2, IgG3.3D7 or IgG2.DBL5.0466 antibody. This indicated that there are multiple mechanisms for antibodies to confer protection.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with inference about multiple protective mechanisms.

claim: Antibody features that were higher in women with non-placental infection compared to those with placental malaria included DBL2-specific IgG3, IgA2, IgG2, and IgG4 as well as DBL3-specific antibodies that bind FcγRIIIb and DBL5-specific IgG2 and IgG4.
source: Antibody features that were higher in women with non-placental infection compared to those with placental malaria included DBL2-specific IgG3, IgA2, IgG2, and IgG4 (IgG3.DBL2(ID1-ID2a).FCR3, IgA2.DBL2.1010, IgG2.DBL2(ID1-ID2a).FCR3, and IgG4.DBL2.1010, respectively) as well as DBL3-specific antibodies that bind FcγRIIIb (FcγRIIIB.DBL3.FCR3) and DBL5-specific IgG2 and IgG4 (IgG2.DBL5.0466 and IgG4.DBL5.0466).
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing univariate comparisons.

claim: DBL2, DBL3, and DBL5 were selected for the assessment of functional antibody features using cell-based assays.
source: Thus, we selected DBL2, DBL3, and DBL5 for the assessment of functional antibody features using cell-based assays in order to provide insights into the mechanistic contribution of these enhanced antibody populations.
evidence: This is stated in the results section describing the rationale for selecting specific DBL domains.

claim: Antibody responses did not significantly differ between non-infected and placental malaria groups.
source: As antibody responses did not significantly differ between non-infected and placental malaria groups, further data analysis was restricted to those 77 women with non-placental infection or with placental malaria.
evidence: This is stated in the results section explaining the rationale for focusing on two groups.

claim: The lack of differences in antibody features between the non-infected and placental malaria groups may be attributable to the heterogeneous nature of the non-infected group.
